scenarios.description: General knowledge question — answered, not 'no record'
outputs:
TCP and UDP are both transport-layer protocols, but they trade off reliability against speed.

**TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)**
- Connection-oriented — establishes a session via a three-way handshake before data flows
- Guarantees delivery: lost packets are retransmitted
- Preserves ordering — data arrives in the sequence it was sent
- Includes flow control and congestion control
- Higher overhead and latency
- Used for HTTP/HTTPS, SSH, SMTP, file transfer

**UDP (User Datagram Protocol)**
- Connectionless — packets ("datagrams") are simply sent
- No delivery guarantee, no retransmission
- No ordering guarantee
- No flow or congestion control built in
- Minimal overhead, lower latency
- Used for DNS, VoIP, video streaming, gaming, QUIC (which layers its own reliability on top)

The short version: choose TCP when every byte must arrive correctly and in order; choose UDP when timeliness matters more than completeness, or when you want to implement your own reliability logic.

scenarios.description: No hollow opener — no 'Certainly', 'Of course', 'Great question'
outputs:
Continuous integration (CI) is the practice of merging developers' work into a shared mainline frequently — typically several times a day — with each merge automatically verified by a build and test run.

The core elements:

- **Shared mainline** — everyone integrates into the same branch rather than maintaining long-lived feature branches
- **Automated build** — every commit triggers a compile and packaging step
- **Automated tests** — unit and integration tests run on each build to catch regressions immediately
- **Fast feedback** — builds are kept short so failures surface within minutes
- **Fix-first culture** — a broken build takes priority over new work

The point is to avoid "integration hell", where divergent branches become painful to merge. Small, frequent integrations keep conflicts trivial and make defects easy to trace to the commit that caused them.

Common tooling includes GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, and Buildkite. CI is usually the precursor to continuous delivery, where a passing build is automatically deployable.
